title: AI concept art vs actual gameplay: how do you test readability before accepting an effect?
author: AbyssChronicles_Game
selftext:
We're the developer account for ABYSS CHRONICLES, a solo-developed deep-sea hack-and-slash ARPG with six playable races. We use Claude for implementation and Codex for visual work, checks and tooling; AI-assisted art is part of the project.



The awkward part of this workflow is deciding when an image is a target and when it is evidence of the game. A polished concept can make an unfinished effect look finished. Our current rule is to keep concept images labelled separately and use actual in-engine footage for gameplay claims. The effects are still being reworked; we're not treating a strong concept as proof of readable combat.



For the six-race pitch, the question we're trying to answer is whether players can identify each race's action from a short clip without a label. That's a test we want to pass, not a result we're claiming.



If you use generated art or AI-assisted effects, what is your most useful in-engine check before accepting an asset: silhouette at gameplay scale, enemy telegraph visibility, or something else? I'd be interested in concrete tests you've rejected an asset over.



The current project is on Steam: [https://store.steampowered.com/app/5384220/?utm\_source=reddit&utm\_medium=community&utm\_campaign=abyss&utm\_content=ai\_readability\_20261019](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5384220/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=community&utm_campaign=abyss&utm_content=ai_readability_20261019)



Work in progress; this is our own commercial game.

comments.author: ZymzAlchemy
comments.body: Human play testing is the only way to be sure.

replies.author: AbyssChronicles_Game
replies.body: Agreed. I'd want to watch someone unfamiliar with the game react to an enemy wind-up without coaching, then ask what they noticed. If it only becomes clear after an explanation, a clean-looking clip hasn't proved anything.
